evidence.limitations: No system-package-manager (apt/brew/choco/winget) or container-registry presence could be confirmed for Quidra as of the snapshot; absence was treated as a rubric-defined low sub-score rather than N/A. Release-cadence evidence covers only the short observed history in the live repository; it is recorded as descriptive cadence data per the frozen spec's prohibition on using elapsed time/age as a direct threshold or bonus/penalty.

raw_findings: Packaging is produced by CPack per platform: Linux DEB/TGZ, macOS TGZ, Windows ZIP, confirmed on the quidra-lang/quidra README build section.

GitHub Releases are created automatically by a CI workflow ('github-actions released this') for v0.1.0, v0.2.0, v0.3.0 (6 assets each) and v0.3.1 (4 assets), i.e. multiple platform artifacts are actually published per tagged release, not just source tarballs.

docs/development.md step 7-8 requires the release workflow to 'create the GitHub Release and all supported platform artifacts' before a release counts as complete, and step 9 requires the release tag, main version metadata, packaged 'quidra --version', and published assets to all agree.

README build-from-source instructions give explicit CMake commands and exact native dependency list (Clang 15+, libcurl, libpng/libjpeg/libtiff/libwebp dev files) for Linux, with a separate Windows (vcpkg-based) path.

No evidence was found of Quidra being distributed through a hosted system/community package-manager channel (apt repository, Homebrew formula, Chocolatey/winget, Docker Hub image, or a language-native registry such as npm/cargo/pip) as of the snapshot date; the DEB artifact is a local install package, not a hosted apt feed.

docs/packages.md: the first-party library installer ('quidra install ...') resolves only immutable exact 'vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH' git tags, never main/develop/feature branches, checks each tag's manifest before cloning, and never executes an install script.

Asset-backed package installs are HTTPS-only, require curl/tar, and the installer 'inspects the archive before extraction, rejects absolute/traversing paths, links, and attempts to replace main.qui, quidra.package, .git, or quidra.lock' before an atomic publish.

quidra.lock version 3 records distribution name, import name, version, and a SHA-256 content hash for every direct/transitive package, and compilation checks both version and hash, giving reproducible, verifiable installs of the package ecosystem (not the compiler itself).

docs/development.md's single-source-of-truth metadata check (sync_metadata.py --check, run in CI and again before tagging) verifies that the CMake/Debian toolchain minimums, README build-requirement prose, and 'the repository the installer script downloads from' all agree with project.toml, reducing drift between documented and actual install requirements.
metric.installation_distribution_experie.rubric: Frozen 5-part rubric (20 pts each, same criteria intended for all 10 languages): (1) availability of automated prebuilt/installable artifacts across major desktop OSes; (2) presence in third-party/system package-manager channels (apt repo, Homebrew, Chocolatey/winget, Docker, language-native registries); (3) quality/clarity of documented build-from-source path incl. explicit dependency versions; (4) maturity/safety of the project's own package/dependency installer UX; (5) release-artifact verifiability and consistency automation.
metric.installation_distribution_experie.score_rationale: Quidra scores above the rubric midpoint: it has automated, verifiable multi-platform release artifacts (DEB/TGZ/ZIP via CPack, produced by a CI-driven GitHub Release workflow with consistency checks across README/manifest/CLI/tag) and a genuinely mature, security-conscious first-party package installer (tag-only resolution, no arbitrary script execution, HTTPS-only signed-shape asset merging, SHA-256 lockfile verification). It loses points because there is no evidence of presence in any hosted system/community package-manager channel (no apt repo, Homebrew, Chocolatey/winget, or container image), so most non-expert users must either build from source or manually fetch a GitHub Release asset rather than using a familiar one-line installer or OS package manager.

raw_findings: docs/development.md defines an explicit SemVer policy for the pre-1.0 language: 'X.0 is appropriate for new language features... X.Y is appropriate for compatible fixes... 1.0.0 is reserved for the first explicitly stable language contract', and states a `-dev`/`-rc` suffix is rejected by the parser and CMake.

The release procedure (docs/development.md) requires green CI on develop (full test suite), merging into main, re-verified main CI, and only then an automated 'release' workflow on push to main that re-checks derived metadata, refuses to continue if the tag already exists, and creates/pushes the immutable tag itself — tags are explicitly never created by hand or from develop/feature branches.

Release checks required before a release counts as complete include GCC and Clang builds, Linux/macOS/Windows CI, sanitizer and warnings-as-errors builds, ctest, parser/checker negative tests, native runtime smoke tests, package/version/lockfile tests, REPL/CLI tests, packaging tests, the metadata SSOT check, and version-consistency checks.
'The release tag is immutable. Never force-move, delete/recreate, or reuse a published vX.Y.Z tag for different source... superseded by a new... release, never by retargeting the existing tag.'

Format versions (device ABI, typed IR, package-manifest schema, lockfile schema) are declared independently in project.toml and are deliberately decoupled from the product release version; a package's declared requires.abi is enforced exactly against the compiler's abi_version via the PACKAGE_COMPATIBILITY diagnostic, and requires.quidra semver ranges are enforced at install/compile time.

quidra.lock format itself evolved (v1/v2/v3) while remaining backward-readable: 'Version-1 and version-2 lockfiles remain readable for compatibility; rewriting the lockfile upgrades it to version 3', showing a documented compatibility-preserving migration path rather than a breaking change.

Observed actual releases (quidra-lang/quidra GitHub Releases) as of the snapshot: v0.1.0, v0.2.0 (with a documented PR trail showing the develop HEAD passed 'the repository CI matrix, including GCC/Clang, sanitizers, macOS, Windows, packaging and image dtype coverage' before promotion), v0.3.0, and a v0.3.1 patch release, each produced by an automated github-actions release with a linked Full Changelog and, for v0.2.0, a GitHub-verified signed commit.

A dedicated first-party-package compatibility CI ('Add first-party package compatibility CI') continuously tests the released vision/dnn packages against core changes before they land in develop/main, so downstream package breakage is caught pre-release rather than discovered post-release.

The four observed releases occurred within a span of days rather than months, showing an active but very young release history; this is recorded as descriptive cadence evidence (not used as an age penalty) and slightly tempers confidence in long-run stability despite the strong process controls.
metric.toolchain_stability_release_matur.rubric: Frozen 5-part rubric (20 pts each): (1) documented, followed Semantic Versioning policy with explicit meaning per version segment; (2) release reproducibility/CI gating strength (compilers, OSes, sanitizers, negative tests, packaging tests) required before a tag exists; (3) immutability/non-retargeting guarantees for published releases; (4) explicit compatibility contracts (ABI/IR/schema versioning, package compatibility enforcement) independent of the product version; (5) observed maintenance/release cadence and consistency across actual releases. Language age/first-release date are excluded as scoring inputs per the frozen ecosystem spec.
metric.toolchain_stability_release_matur.score_rationale: Quidra scores well above the rubric midpoint on process-based release maturity: it has a clearly documented, consistently followed SemVer policy, an unusually strict CI-gated and fully automated tag/release procedure with explicit tag-immutability guarantees, and independently versioned/enforced ABI-IR-schema compatibility contracts plus a backward-compatible lockfile-format migration path. It is not scored at the top of the rubric because the only observable release history is four releases within a few days, which demonstrates active automation and gating but not yet a long-run track record of sustained cadence, support windows for older minor lines, or a stable (post-1.0) compatibility contract.
